West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said 17 people were brought dead to Medical College and Hospital, Kolkata, while a child died at R.G. Jairam Ramesh said the ECI’s October 15, 2026, order to share “readable” electoral rolls with parties — after refusing the demand since 2018 — came because “ the whole nation is on the streets against the Vote Chors.” He said CEC Gyanesh Kumar, acting on instructions from PM Modi and Home Minister Shah, “simply has to go,” and the SIR, which he said put 13 crore Indians’ voting rights at risk, must be suspended immediately. #### Seven, including Chorbagan Durga Puja organisers, arrested for pandal stampede in Kolkata: Police Seven people, including the secretary and vice president of the Chorbagan Sarbajanin Durga Puja committee, have been arrested in connection with the pandal stampede that killed at least 19 people, said the Kolkata Police on Sunday (October 18, 2026). Two security in-charges and one person who was in charge of construction work have also been arrested, among others, the officials said. #### Adhikari orders independent probe, promises compensation for victims’ families West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari, after meeting the victims of the stampede in the Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata, said that the Government will take responsibility for the tragedy and launch an independent probe by a fact-finding team, headed by a sitting judge. #### 14 killed, 40 injured as truck hits devotees near temple in Madhya Pradesh’s Gwalior At least 14 people, including two women and two teenagers, were killed in Madhya Pradesh’s Gwalior after an out-of-control truck entered a prohibited zone and rammed into a crowd of devotees near a famous temple in the early hours of Sunday (October 18, 2026), officials said. More than 40 people were injured in the accident.

items.title: Inflation is retreating from most of the store — why your biggest bills are the holdouts: Chart of the Day
items.excerpt: Inflation is retreating from most of the store — why your biggest bills are the holdouts: Chart of the Day # Inflation is retreating from most of the store — why your biggest bills are the holdouts: Chart of the Day Jared Blikre Sun, October 18, 2026 at 6:33 AM CDT 3 min read Inflation is reaching fewer corners of the economy. That doesn't mean life is getting cheaper. Only about 38% of the roughly 175 categories in the Consumer Price Index rose faster than a 3% annual pace over the past six months, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data. That's down from 56% in May and the fewest since spring 2025. The count borrows a test from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who laid it out at Jackson Hole in August. He counts how many categories in the Fed's preferred PCE price gauge are rising faster than 3%, a gauge of how widespread inflation is. The Fed's goal is still 2%. BLS, Yahoo Finance "Too many categories are still posting increases above 3% on both a six- and 12-month basis," Warsh said after the Fed raised rates in September. By that yardstick, September looked better than its hotter-than-expected headline. The 12-month count slipped to about 47% from 51% in August. At the 2022 peak, about 4 in 5 categories topped 3%. In the two decades before the pandemic, about 1 in 3 typically did. A narrower spread strengthens the case for waiting, and traders have leaned that way. The bond market put the odds of a hike at the Oct. 27-28 meeting at about 17% by Friday's close, according to Bloomberg data — down from roughly 33% after Wednesday's CPI report. Warsh declined to preview his next move in remarks Friday before the International Monetary Fund. Some Fed officials want more evidence before moving. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called September's inflation report discouraging but told Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger he favors waiting before acting again. "We need to get more data," he said. ## The holdout categories are the expensive ones Electricity, rent, hospital services, and car repairs have all been rising faster than 3% over the past six months, after adjusting for seasonal swings. Gasoline is up about 34% from a year ago. Together, the categories still above the line make up at least 60% of the CPI basket, which the BLS weights by how much households spend on each item. Groceries show the other side of the problem. Grocery prices rose less than 2% over the past year, yet they're still up nearly a third since December 2019. Electricity is up 43% over the same stretch. BLS, Yahoo Finance Slower inflation means prices rise more slowly. It doesn't bring them back down, and the Fed has no intention of returning to 2019 prices. Not everyone sees progress. "There is little evidence of a cooling or a broad-based disinflationary impulse," RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas wrote Wednesday, pointing to trade, energy, and AI as sources of stubborn price pressure. He expects another quarter-point hike in December. The bond market leans his way on the longer view. Traders still price in about one full quarter-point increase by the Dec. 9 meeting and nearly three by September 2027. The next test arrives Oct. 29, when September PCE inflation is released, one day after the Fed decides. Next month's CPI report follows. If the six-month count holds below 40%, the case for waiting gets stronger. A return to 50% or more — near where it sat for most of the first half of the year — would put a hike back on the table. Watch rent and electricity. Until they cool, a shrinking count won't feel like relief. *Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication.* *Jared Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance. Follow him on X at @SPYJared or email him at **jaredblikre@yahooinc.com**.*

items.title: Poll: Americans are anxious, pessimistic and deeply ...
items.excerpt: Weeks ahead of Election Day, 71% of U.S. adults think the country is on the “wrong track.” It’s the highest share yet in President Donald Trump’s second term, illustrating the grim national mood his party faces in the midterm elections, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey. ... Poll respondents expressed deep unhappiness over economic conditions and widespread distrust toward both major political parties, but Trump and Republicans bore the brunt. For the first time in Trump’s second term, the poll has found the “right track” sinking into the 20s. A majority of Americans view the president’s administration as uniquely corrupt, even as they look skeptically at corruption in both parties. And they say Trump is failing to improve their material financial conditions. ... Trump’s approval rating slipped to 34% among U.S. adults, a second-term low in this poll, while his disapproval rating rose to 66%. In another warning sign, the poll found a majority (51%) of respondents “strongly disapprove” of his performance, a second-term high. ... Trump’s approval rating is slightly better among registered voters, 39%-61%. Registered voters said they prefer Democrats over Republicans to control Congress by a 55%-45% spread, another sign that the GOP’s House and Senate majorities are in danger in the Nov. 3 election. ... Yet despite the sinking ratings for the party in power, Americans continue to hold a negative view of Democrats, too. Among adults, just 43% view the Democratic Party favorably, while 57% hold an unfavorable view. ... Economic concerns are at the center of the sour national mood, with the economy once again topping the list of most important issues at 31%. While 18% of Americans said their financial situation is better off today than a year ago, 38% said it’s about the same and 44% said it’s worse now. ... Trump has sought to appeal to voters by promising $5,000 payments if Republicans win the 2026 midterms. But the new poll showed that most U.S. adults aren’t buying it: Just 14% said they “definitely” or “probably” expect to receive such a check if the GOP keeps control of Congress, while 71% think they “definitely” or “probably” won’t.

items.title: Ukraine and the U.S. are at odds over Starshield. Here's ...
items.excerpt: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and U.S. officials remain at odds over disruptions to a key satellite communications service used by the Ukrainian military. Zelenskyy told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday he believes the U.S. government is behind his military's loss of normal access to the Starshield and Starlink services, claiming tech firm SpaceX imposed the restrictions in response to a "message from [the] American government." Warning that the U.S. siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake," the Ukrainian leader claimed that the Starshield system has not been fully restored, despite what U.S. government officials have said publicly. In a post on X over the weekend, Zelenskyy said the restrictions on the system have hindered Ukraine's ability to intercept weapons launched by Russia, calling the consequences "very painful and unpleasant." ... Starlink is a satellite internet network operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX to provide internet service to the U.S. and other counties. Since 2024, the U.S. Defense Department has shared a high-powered military version of the network called Starshield with Ukraine, which has cost the Pentagon billions of dollars. Ukraine relies on the network in its defenses against Russia's nearly five-year full-scale war. ... Zelenskyy said the disruptions to Starshield came without warning last week. He told NPR in an interview that losing normal access to the critical defense network had left his military's frontlines vulnerable. On X over the weekend, he said the network's speed hasn't been fully restored. It's unclear why Ukraine has experienced restricted access to Starshield. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that the U.S. government is responsible for the system, and that "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." A bipartisan group of senators is calling on the Defense Department's inspector general to investigate how the system was disrupted. ### State Department reaction ... Speaking to reporters on Friday, President Trump denied interfering with Starshield. "I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon. And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been," he said. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also rejected Zelenskyy's claims that the disruptions to the system were deliberate. ... "It's just categorically false. No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn't use it," Rubio told reporters on Saturday, adding that Ukraine requested access to the system to carry out strikes deep inside Russia. "That's under conversation. It's under discussion right now of how they would want to use it," he said. ... The Starshield disruptions have renewed questions over the United States' commitment to supporting Ukraine against Russia's war, with tensions between President Trump and Zelenskyy growing over the past few days. ... Earlier this month, Trump moved to ease U.S. sanctions against Russia that had been passed by Congress. After Zelenskyy pushed back on the move, calling it a "weak decision by strong partners," Trump lashed out, criticizing Ukraine for striking Russian refineries, which he said was affecting U.S. diesel prices. "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," Trump said. ... The war of words has continued in the past few days, with the Ukrainian president outlining further areas of disagreement. On Sunday's Meet the Press, Zelenskyy also said that U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine concerning Russia ballistic missile attacks was blocked for three days, but has resumed. ... Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Russia has launched more than 4,000 strike drones, bombs and missiles against his country over the past week. Russian attacks on Saturday night targeted energy substations leaving tens of thousands of people without electricity, according to Zelenskyy.

items.title: Harry Styles Enlists John Wilson for Documentary About MSG Residency
items.excerpt: Harry Styles has enlisted filmmaker John Wilson to make a documentary about the singer’s current Madison Square Garden residency. In recent days, photos of Wilson — the offbeat documentarian behind his own How To With John Wilson HBO series and The History of Concrete — trailing Styles with camera in hand emerged on social media, leading fans to wonder if the two were collaborating on some sort of project. ... Variety has confirmed that the project in question is a documentary about Styles’ Together, Together 30-show residency at MSG, which started in August — when Wilson began filming — and runs through October 31. Not a traditional documentarian, Wilson’s Styles film will feature “a hybrid of live performances and a glimpse into Styles’ world,” Variety reported, adding that Wilson will dig deep into the residency with “authentic human stories of everyone involved in the tour —from the singer and his fans to countless others behind the scenes.” ... Universal Pictures Content Group, Peanut World Pictures and Styles are producing the documentary, with a theatrical release potentially in the works.

items.title: Tini: FUTTURA World Tour | Miami & Miami Beach
items.excerpt: Argentine pop artist Tini brings her FUTTURA World Tour to downtown Miami for the tour’s only U.S. stop. Tini: FUTTURA World Tour takes place Sunday, October 18, 2026 at Kaseya Center. The tour is described as a retrospective project spanning Tini’s different musical eras, from her early international breakthrough on Disney Channel Latin America’s Violetta to her solo career in pop, urbano, cumbia and alternative pop. The Miami concert follows the tour’s launch in Buenos Aires and brings the arena production to a U.S. audience for one night only. Born Martina Stoessel, Tini is an Argentine singer, actress and performer whose albums include Tini, Quiero Volver, Tini Tini Tini, Cupido and Un Mechón de Pelo. Her career includes chart success in Latin America and Europe, multiple major music awards and collaborations that have expanded her reach across Latin pop and global music audiences. The event is open to all ages, though ages 18 and older are recommended.
